title: All's Well That Ends Well
primary_sources: William Painter, The Palace of Pleasure (1566), novel 38
setting: Rousillon, Paris, Florence, and Marseilles
synopsis_short: Helena, a poor physician's orphan, loves the noble Bertram far above her rank. She cures the dying King of France and is granted Bertram as her reward, but he refuses the marriage and flees to the wars, vowing to accept her only when she wins his ring and bears his child—conditions he thinks impossible. By the bed-trick Helena fulfils both and claims him at last.

title: The Tragedy of Antony and Cleopatra
setting: Rome, Alexandria, and the eastern Mediterranean (40–30 BCE)
synopsis_short: Mark Antony, one of Rome's three rulers, neglects his duties for Cleopatra, queen of Egypt. His rivalry with the cold young Octavius Caesar pulls him home to a marriage of alliance, but he returns to Egypt and war follows. Beaten at Actium and falsely told Cleopatra is dead, Antony falls on his sword; she follows by the asp's bite rather than grace Caesar's triumph.

title: As You Like It
setting: A usurper's court and the Forest of Arden
synopsis_short: Orlando, kept down by his elder brother, and Rosalind, banished by her usurping uncle, both flee to the Forest of Arden. Disguised as the youth 'Ganymede,' Rosalind meets the lovesick Orlando and offers to cure him by having him woo 'Ganymede' as if it were she. Among shepherds, a clown, and the melancholy Jaques, four couples are matched and the usurper converted.

title: The Comedy of Errors
date_first_performed: 28 December 1594 (the Gray's Inn revels — the 'Night of Errors')
primary_sources: Plautus, Amphitruo (the twin servants and the locked-out husband)
setting: The city of Ephesus, over a single day
synopsis_short: Two sets of identical twins — masters and servants, separated by a shipwreck in infancy — land in Ephesus on the same day. As the travelling Antipholus and his Dromio are everywhere mistaken for their resident doubles, an afternoon dissolves into beatings, a locked-out husband, a disputed gold chain, an arrest, charges of madness and witchcraft, and a family reunion at the priory.

title: The Tragedy of Coriolanus
setting: Republican Rome and the Volscian cities of Corioli and Antium
synopsis_short: Caius Marcius, Rome's fiercest soldier, wins the surname Coriolanus by storming the Volscian city of Corioli, but his contempt for the common people and his refusal to court their votes turn the tribunes and the crowd against him. Banished, he joins his old enemy Aufidius and marches on Rome, relenting only when his mother begs him to spare the city — a mercy that costs him his life.

title: The Tragedy of Cymbeline
primary_sources: The Rare Triumphs of Love and Fortune (anon., c. 1582)
setting: Ancient Britain (the court and the Welsh mountains) and Renaissance Rome
synopsis_short: Banished for marrying the king's daughter Imogen, Posthumus is tricked by the Italian Iachimo into believing her unfaithful and orders her killed. Disguised as a boy, Imogen flees toward Wales, where her long-lost royal brothers live in a cave. Through a Roman invasion, a vision of the god Jupiter, and a cascade of revelations, the scattered family and two kingdoms are reconciled.

title: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
setting: Elsinore, royal court of Denmark
synopsis_short: A Danish prince, ordered by his murdered father's ghost to avenge the crime, delays and disintegrates while the court around him does the same.

title: The First Part of Henry the Fourth
primary_sources: The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth (anon., c. 1586)
setting: England and Wales, 1402–1403 (ending at the Battle of Shrewsbury)
synopsis_short: While rebels rise against Henry IV, the King's tavern-haunting son Prince Hal bides his time among thieves before redeeming himself and killing the rebel hero Hotspur at the Battle of Shrewsbury.

title: The Second Part of Henry the Fourth
primary_sources: Samuel Daniel, The First Four Books of the Civil Wars (1595)
The Famous Victories of Henry V (anonymous, pre-1594)
setting: England, 1403–1413: from the aftermath of Shrewsbury to the death of Henry IV and Hal's accession
synopsis_short: As Henry IV sickens and the northern rebellion sputters to its treacherous end at Gaultree, Prince Hal lingers a last while among Falstaff and the Eastcheap crowd — until, crowned at his father's death, he rejects the old knight and embraces the rule of law.

title: The Life of Henry the Fifth
primary_sources: The Famous Victories of Henry V (anonymous, pre-1594)
Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families (1548)
setting: England and France, leading to and through Agincourt (1415)
synopsis_short: Crowned and transformed, the former Prince Hal revives England's claim to France, foils a treasonous plot, and leads a sick, outnumbered army to a stunning victory at Agincourt — while a Chorus bids us imagine the 'vasty fields of France' on a bare stage. It ends in his blunt wooing of the French princess.

title: The First Part of Henry the Sixth
primary_sources: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families (1548)
setting: England and France, 1422–1444: the boy-king's reign and the loss of the French conquests
synopsis_short: As Henry V is buried, his infant son inherits a France that begins to slip away. The heroic Talbot fights on while Joan la Pucelle rallies the French and the English nobles fall to feuding — above all in the Temple Garden, where plucking red and white roses seeds the Wars of the Roses. The squabbling lords leave Talbot to die, and Suffolk woos Margaret of Anjou for the boy king.

title: The Second Part of Henry the Sixth
primary_sources: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families (1548)
setting: England, 1445–1455: from Margaret's arrival to the outbreak of the Wars of the Roses at the first battle of St Albans
synopsis_short: Margaret of Anjou arrives as queen, and her favourite Suffolk schemes with Cardinal Beaufort and the Duke of York to destroy 'good Duke Humphrey' of Gloucester. Gloucester is murdered and Suffolk banished; York foments Jack Cade's bloody commoners' revolt as a trial of strength, then returns from Ireland in arms to open the Wars of the Roses at St Albans.

title: The Third Part of Henry the Sixth
primary_sources: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families (1548)
setting: England and France, 1455–1471: from the Yorkist victory at St Albans through Wakefield and Towton, Edward IV's accession, Warwick's revolt, to the murder of Henry VI in the Tower
synopsis_short: After St Albans, York forces King Henry to name him heir, disinheriting Henry's son. War erupts: York is captured and killed by Margaret, but his sons avenge him and Edward seizes the crown as Edward IV. His rash marriage turns Warwick the Kingmaker against him; Warwick restores Henry, then dies at Barnet. The Yorkists win at Tewkesbury, and Richard of Gloucester murders Henry in the Tower.

title: The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth
date_first_performed: 1613 (the Globe burned down during a performance on 29 June 1613)
primary_sources: Hall, The Union of the Two Noble Families (1548)
setting: England under Henry VIII (c. 1520–1533)
synopsis_short: Cardinal Wolsey rises to dominate Henry VIII and destroys the Duke of Buckingham, but his pride and secret double-dealing bring him crashing down. Henry sets aside Queen Katherine — who defends herself with unanswerable dignity — to marry Anne Bullen. The play closes with the christening of their daughter Elizabeth and a prophecy of her glorious reign.

title: The Life and Death of King John
primary_sources: The Troublesome Raigne of King John (anon., 1591)
setting: England and France, early 13th century
synopsis_short: King John holds the English crown against the claim of his young nephew Arthur, backed by France. After war, a brief marriage-peace, and the Pope's interdict, John has Arthur imprisoned and orders his death; Hubert spares him, but the boy dies escaping. England's lords revolt and France invades; the tide turns, John is poisoned by a monk, and his son succeeds.

title: The Tragedy of Julius Caesar
setting: Rome, Sardis, and the plains of Philippi (44–42 BCE)
synopsis_short: A conspiracy of senators, fearing Caesar means to make himself king, draws the honorable Brutus into assassinating him on the ides of March; Mark Antony's funeral oration turns Rome against the killers, and the ensuing civil war destroys Brutus and Cassius at Philippi.

title: The Tragedy of King Lear
primary_sources: The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir (anon., 1605)
Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae
setting: Legendary ancient Britain
synopsis_short: Old King Lear divides Britain between the two daughters who flatter him and disowns Cordelia, the one who loves him truly. Cast out by Goneril and Regan, he goes mad in a storm; in a mirroring plot, the Earl of Gloucester is blinded after trusting his treacherous bastard son Edmund. Cordelia's rescue comes too late: she is hanged, and Lear dies of grief over her body.

title: A Lover's Complaint
setting: A riverside in the country
synopsis_short: Printed in 1609 with the Sonnets: a narrator overhears a 'fickle maid' lament how a beautiful, eloquent young man seduced and abandoned her — and confesses that his arts would seduce her all over again. A 'complaint' poem shadowing the Sonnets' themes.

title: Love's Labour's Lost
date_first_performed: before 1598 (the 1598 quarto says it was 'presented before her Highness this last Christmas')
primary_sources: No known direct narrative source — one of Shakespeare's most original plots
Topical: the courtiers' names echo figures of the contemporary French court (Henri of Navarre and the ducs de Biron, Longueville, and Mayenne)
setting: The park of the King of Navarre's court
synopsis_short: The King of Navarre and three lords swear a three-year oath to study, fast, and shun women — then fall in love the moment the Princess of France and her ladies arrive. Their witty wooing, disguises, and a pageant of the Nine Worthies are cut short by news of the French king's death; the ladies impose a year's penance, and the play ends, unusually, with love's labour postponed.

title: The Tragedy of Macbeth
setting: Scotland (and England), 11th century
synopsis_short: A Scottish general, prophesied by three witches to become king, murders his kinsman King Duncan in his sleep and seizes the throne. To keep it he kills again and again, while his wife is destroyed by guilt; equivocating prophecies lull him until Birnam Wood marches on Dunsinane and Macduff, 'not of woman born,' cuts him down.

title: Measure for Measure
setting: Vienna
synopsis_short: Duke Vincentio leaves the strict deputy Angelo to govern Vienna and stays disguised as a friar to watch. Angelo revives a dead law and condemns Claudio to death for fornication; when Claudio's novice sister Isabella pleads for him, Angelo demands her chastity as the price. The disguised Duke arranges a bed-trick and a substitute head, then returns to judge — pardons and forced marriages follow.

title: The Comical History of the Merchant of Venice
primary_sources: Fiorentino, Il Pecorone (the flesh-bond and the lady of Belmont, 1558)
Gesta Romanorum (the three caskets; English trans. Robinson, 1577)
setting: Venice and Belmont
synopsis_short: To fund his friend Bassanio's suit to the heiress Portia, the merchant Antonio borrows from the Jewish moneylender Shylock on a bond of a pound of his flesh. Bassanio wins Portia by the casket test, but Antonio's ships are lost and Shylock demands his forfeit. Disguised as a lawyer, Portia saves Antonio and defeats Shylock, who is forced to convert.

title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
setting: Windsor
date_first_performed: by 1597 (traditionally linked to a Garter Feast)
primary_sources: Largely Shakespeare's own invention (the Falstaff frame)
Analogues for the jealous-husband / lover-in-hiding motif in Italian novelle (e.g., Fiorentino, Il Pecorone)
synopsis_short: Short of money, the fat knight Falstaff sends identical love-letters to two married Windsor women, Mistress Ford and Mistress Page. The wives compare notes and gull him three times — dumped in the Thames with the laundry, beaten in disguise, and pinched by mock-fairies at Herne's Oak. Meanwhile their daughter Anne outwits both parents to marry the man she loves.

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
primary_sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book IV (Pyramus and Thisbe)
setting: Athens and a wood nearby
synopsis_short: Four young Athenians chase one another into an enchanted wood, where a quarrel between the fairy king and queen and the mischief of Puck's love-juice tangle their loves; meanwhile a troupe of amateur actors rehearses a play, and one of them is briefly turned into an ass and adored by the fairy queen.

title: Much Ado About Nothing
primary_sources: Ariosto, Orlando Furioso (1516; the Ariodante and Ginevra story)
setting: Messina, on the coast of Sicily
synopsis_short: Soldiers return from war to Governor Leonato's house in Messina. The sharp-witted Beatrice and Benedick, both sworn against marriage, are gulled into loving each other, while young Claudio courts Leonato's daughter Hero. Don Pedro's bastard brother Don John slanders Hero as unchaste, breaking off her wedding; the blundering constable Dogberry and his Watch expose the lie, and both couples wed.

title: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice
primary_sources: Giraldi Cinthio, Gli Hecatommithi, Third Decade, Seventh Novella (1565)
setting: Venice and Cyprus
synopsis_short: In Venice the Moorish general Othello secretly marries Desdemona. His ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, feeds him false 'proof' — a planted handkerchief — that she is unfaithful with the lieutenant Cassio. On Cyprus Othello's jealousy hardens until he smothers Desdemona, then kills himself on learning her innocence and Iago's villainy.

title: The Passionate Pilgrim
synopsis_short: A 1599 poetic miscellany that the printer William Jaggard issued as 'by W. Shakespeare' — but mostly NOT his: only about five of its twenty poems are genuinely Shakespeare's (versions of Sonnets 138 and 144, and three poems from Love's Labour's Lost). The rest are by Marlowe, Barnfield, Griffin, and others. Held back from the reader as an unreliable attribution.

title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
date_published: Q1 1609; omitted from F1 1623; added to F3 1664
primary_sources: Twine, The Patterne of Painefull Adventures (1576)
setting: The eastern Mediterranean: Tyre, Antioch, Tarsus, Pentapolis, Ephesus, and Mytilene
synopsis_short: Narrated across many years and countries by the medieval poet Gower, Prince Pericles of Tyre flees a tyrant's deadly secret, wins and seemingly loses his wife Thaisa to a sea-storm, and is parted from his newborn daughter Marina. After Marina survives murder, pirates, and a brothel by sheer virtue, the goddess Diana reunites the scattered family.

title: The Phoenix and the Turtle
synopsis_short: A short, enigmatic funeral poem: the Phoenix (matchless beauty) and the Turtledove (perfect fidelity) die together in a 'mutual flame,' their two selves so merged that they defeat number and reason itself. The birds gather to mourn, and Reason sings a Threnos over their ashes. First printed in Robert Chester's 1601 'Love's Martyr.'

title: The Rape of Lucrece
setting: Rome and Collatium, at the fall of the monarchy
synopsis_short: Shakespeare's grave 1594 companion to Venus and Adonis: Sextus Tarquinius rapes Lucrece, the chaste wife of his comrade; she reveals the crime, exacts an oath of revenge, and kills herself, and Brutus turns the outrage into the revolution that founds the Roman Republic.

title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
setting: England and Wales, 1398–1400
synopsis_short: King Richard II banishes his cousin Bolingbroke and seizes his inheritance; Bolingbroke returns in arms, deposes him, and takes the crown as Henry IV, leaving Richard to fall from anointed king to murdered prisoner.

title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
characters_major: Richard (Duke of Gloucester, later Richard III)
primary_sources: Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513)
Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families (1548)
setting: England, 1471–1485: from the murder of Henry VI to Richard's seizure of the crown and his death at the battle of Bosworth Field
synopsis_short: Deformed and ruthless, Richard of Gloucester schemes toward the throne: he has his brother Clarence murdered, woos Lady Anne over a corpse, and destroys the queen's kindred. Crowned after branding his nephews bastards, he has the two young princes smothered in the Tower. As allies desert him, his victims' ghosts curse him before Bosworth, where Richmond kills him and becomes Henry VII.

title: The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
primary_sources: Brooke, The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562)
setting: Verona and Mantua, Italy
synopsis_short: Two teenagers from feuding Veronese families fall in love, marry in secret, and die in the space of four days.

title: The Taming of the Shrew
primary_sources: George Gascoigne, Supposes (1566; trans. of Ariosto, I Suppositi) — the Bianca subplot
The Taming of A Shrew (anon., printed 1594)
setting: Padua and Petruchio's country house, with an Induction set in the English countryside
synopsis_short: A drunken tinker is gulled into believing he is a lord and sits down to watch a play: in Padua, fortune-hunting Petruchio courts and 'tames' the sharp-tongued Katherina through a campaign of contradiction, while her gentle sister Bianca's disguised suitors compete for her. It ends in a wedding banquet, a wager on the wives, and Katherina's much-debated speech on a wife's duty.

title: The Tempest
primary_sources: Strachey, A True Reportory of the Wracke (1610)
Jourdain, A Discovery of the Barmudas (1610)
setting: A remote island in the Mediterranean
synopsis_short: Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, has lived twelve years on a remote island with his daughter Miranda, served by the airy spirit Ariel and the islander Caliban. When his enemies sail near, he raises a storm to wreck them ashore, guides Miranda and Ferdinand into love, foils two murder plots, and — choosing forgiveness over revenge — reclaims his dukedom and frees Ariel.

title: The Life of Timon of Athens
primary_sources: Plutarch, Life of Antony (the Timon digression) and Life of Alcibiades, trans. North (1579)
setting: Athens and the woods nearby
synopsis_short: Timon, a lavishly generous lord of Athens, ruins himself with gifts and feasts. When his money runs out, every flattering friend refuses him. Enraged at their ingratitude, he curses Athens and exiles himself to a cave, where — digging for roots — he finds gold and showers it on thieves and on the banished Alcibiades, now marching on the city. Timon dies a misanthrope by the sea.

title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus
primary_sources: The History of Titus Andronicus (anonymous prose chapbook)
setting: Rome in its imperial decline, and the forest near it
synopsis_short: Returning victorious over the Goths, the Roman general Titus sacrifices their queen Tamora's eldest son. Made empress, Tamora revenges herself on his family: her sons rape and mutilate his daughter Lavinia and frame his sons for murder, helped by her lover, the Moor Aaron. Feigning madness, Titus repays her with a banquet of her own sons baked in a pie, and the stage fills with the dead.

title: The History of Troilus and Cressida
primary_sources: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (after Boccaccio, Il Filostrato)
Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474)
setting: Troy and the Greek camp before it
synopsis_short: In the war's seventh year, Troilus loves Cressida, brought together by her bawdy uncle Pandarus—until a prisoner exchange sends her to the Greek camp, where she turns to Diomedes as a hidden Troilus watches. Meanwhile the Greeks scheme to rouse the sulking Achilles, and Achilles' men butcher an unarmed Hector: a bitter satire on war, honour, and love.

title: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
date_first_performed: 2 February 1602 (Middle Temple, recorded by John Manningham)
setting: Illyria, a kingdom on the Adriatic coast
synopsis_short: Shipwrecked in Illyria and believing her twin Sebastian drowned, Viola disguises herself as the page 'Cesario' and serves Duke Orsino, who loves the countess Olivia. Sent to woo Olivia for him, Cesario is loved by Olivia while loving Orsino. Meanwhile Olivia's steward Malvolio is gulled into thinking she loves him. Sebastian's arrival untangles the knot: he weds Olivia, and Viola weds Orsino.

title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
primary_sources: Montemayor, Diana Enamorada (the Felix and Felismena story, 1559)
Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour (Titus and Gisippus, 1531)
setting: Verona, the Duke's court at Milan, and a forest between Milan and Mantua
synopsis_short: Two friends, Valentine and Proteus, leave Verona for the Duke's court at Milan. Valentine loves the Duke's daughter Silvia; Proteus, already sworn to Julia, also falls for Silvia and betrays both his friend and his love to win her. Julia follows in disguise as a page. After a troubling forest confrontation, Proteus repents and the two couples are paired off.

title: Venus and Adonis
setting: The English-Ovidian countryside, across a single day
synopsis_short: Shakespeare's 1593 bestseller: the goddess Venus aggressively woos the beautiful, reluctant young hunter Adonis; he breaks away to hunt a boar, is gored to death, and she turns his blood into a flower. A witty, sensuous debate on desire that darkens into grief.

title: The Winter's Tale
primary_sources: Greene, Pandosto, or The Triumph of Time (1588)
setting: The court of Sicilia and the pastoral countryside of Bohemia, spanning sixteen years
synopsis_short: King Leontes of Sicilia is seized by a jealous conviction that his wife Hermione loves his friend Polixenes, and wrecks his own family: his son dies, his wife seemingly dies, and his baby daughter is cast away on the coast of Bohemia. Sixteen years later that daughter, Perdita, is wooed by Polixenes's son; the lost are found, and Hermione's 'statue' comes to life in a scene of wonder.
